name: H3 Image to Video Flash
summary: A 6-step MiniMax H3 clip with synchronized sound from one picture, on the HyperFlow H3 Flash INT8 checkpoint.

source.notes: Built from the exact ComfyUI API graph of the successful HyperFlow H3 Flash INT8 i2v run at multiple=32 (seed 42, 6 steps, 1.0 MP, 16:9). The earlier 1.0 MP run failed because multiple=8 gave an odd 85-wide latent; at multiple=32 the target and the resized first frame are 1376x768.

inputs.label: First frame
inputs.help: The clip starts on this picture. It is resized to the requested width and height.

inputs.label: Prompt
inputs.default:
integrated_multimodal_description:

[Shot 1] 0–15 seconds. Premium live-action American television sitcom, warm contemporary apartment comedy, natural expressive performances, sharp conversational timing, playful romantic tension and subtle studio-audience laughter. Realistic human facial animation, precise dialogue lip synchronization, believable eye contact and relaxed physical comedy.

BEGIN EXACTLY WITH THE PROVIDED IMAGE.

A stylish modern open-plan apartment kitchen under warm evening lighting. A beautiful brunette woman with shoulder-length wavy hair wears a black satin blouse tucked into fitted blue jeans. She stands on the left, holding a smartphone and a stemmed glass of white wine, giving the man beside her an amused, slightly suspicious sideways glance.

On the right stands her handsome dark-haired boyfriend with short facial stubble, wearing a charcoal-grey long-sleeved Henley shirt, dark jeans and a wristwatch. His left hand rests casually inside his trouser pocket while his right hand holds a black smartphone. He is smiling mischievously at the screen.

Behind them, a white marble kitchen island holds a wine bottle, two additional wine glasses and a small set of keys. Stainless-steel appliances, dark cabinets, pendant lights and a cozy living room complete the background.

Preserve both actors' exact facial identities, clothing, hairstyles, positions, body proportions, handheld objects and apartment layout from the reference image.

0.0–2.0s — THE SETUP:
The scene begins with the exact composition of the reference image. The man reads something amusing on his smartphone and lets out a small, satisfied chuckle. The woman notices his expression and raises one eyebrow while holding her wine glass. He looks up from the phone toward her, clearly excited about his discovery.

2.0–5.0s — THE APP:
The man (S1), speaking with an enthusiastic, slightly smug American male voice, says:

<d>[English] I downloaded an app that predicts our arguments.</d>

He proudly raises his smartphone slightly, as if presenting an extraordinary technological achievement. His eyebrows lift with childish excitement. The woman looks at him with growing disbelief.

5.0–7.3s — THE RESPONSE:
The woman (S2), speaking in a dry, sarcastic American female voice with effortless comedic delivery, replies:

<d>[English] What a waste of money.</d>

She takes a small, casual sip of white wine, completely unimpressed. The man immediately looks down at his phone.

7.3–9.2s — THE FIRST PUNCHLINE:
A tiny cheerful notification chime comes from the man's smartphone.

He looks surprised for a fraction of a second, then slowly breaks into a delighted grin.

The man (S1) says:

<d>[English] It predicted that.</d>

A brief burst of natural studio-audience laughter follows.

9.2–11.0s — THE WARNING:
The woman's smile disappears. She gives him a long, perfectly deadpan stare.

The woman (S2) says, firmly:

<d>[English] Delete it.</d>

She lowers her wine glass slightly without looking away from him.

11.0–12.4s — THE SECOND PUNCHLINE:
The smartphone immediately makes the exact same cheerful notification sound.

The man glances down at his screen, then looks directly at her with an increasingly ridiculous, delighted smile.

The man (S1) says quietly:

<d>[English] That too.</d>

12.4–15.0s — THE SITCOM BUTTON:
The woman freezes, staring at him in complete disbelief. She slowly closes her eyes, takes one controlled breath, then drinks from her wine glass with an expression of profound regret about her life choices.

The man realizes he may have pushed his luck too far. His smug grin slowly collapses into an awkward, nervous smile. Without moving his left hand from his pocket, he carefully lowers the smartphone and looks away, pretending nothing happened.

A perfectly timed warm studio-audience laugh swells at his expression.

Hold the two characters in the same composition until the final frame. End on the awkward silence and the woman's magnificent deadpan expression.

CAMERA AND PERFORMANCE CONTROL:
Single continuous medium-wide sitcom shot, preserving the reference image framing. A very subtle, almost imperceptible camera push-in over the entire scene. No hard cuts, no dramatic camera movement, no close-ups of smartphone screens.

Natural American sitcom performance with witty conversational pacing, expressive eyebrows, small reaction beats, genuine eye contact and controlled physical comedy.

Both actors must speak only their assigned lines. Accurate lip synchronization, no overlapping dialogue, no invented dialogue, no narration.

Preserve the smartphone in the man's right hand, his left hand in his pocket, and the wine glass in the woman's hand. No object teleportation or wardrobe changes.

overall_soundscape:
Natural warm apartment room tone, subtle refrigerator hum, faint clothing movement, gentle wine-glass handling. The man's brief opening chuckle is audible. Two identical bright, short smartphone notification chimes occur at approximately 7.3 and 11 seconds. Carefully timed studio-audience laughter follows the first punchline and builds more strongly after the final punchline. All spoken dialogue remains perfectly clear and prominent. No exaggerated cartoon effects.

non_diegetic_music:
Authentic contemporary American television sitcom sound design. No continuous background music during the conversation. Let the dialogue, smartphone notification chimes, natural comedic pauses and restrained audience laughter carry the scene. A very short, tasteful upbeat sitcom musical sting may punctuate the final reaction during the last half-second.
inputs.help: Describe the motion, the sound and any spoken words. The model resizes the picture to the requested width and height.

options.label: HyperFlow H3 Flash fl2va INT8 (15.9 GB)

inputs.label: Resolution (MP)
inputs.help: Total pixels of the clip, 0.1–3.0 MP. At 16:9 and 1.0 MP, 1376x768 with size multiple 32.

inputs.label: Upscale
inputs.help: Optional RelayVSR pass on the decoded frames before encoding. None keeps the native result; x2/x4 use the matching DIT and Flash VAE, and x4 multiplies pixels by 16 and is slow.

inputs.label: Upscale detail
inputs.help: RelayVSR: how much of what the Flash decoder adds on top of a plain bicubic upscale is kept. 1 is the full model output, lower is calmer and closer to the source.

inputs.label: Size multiple

options.label: 8 (1360x768 at 1.0 MP; can break image conditioning)

inputs.help: Sides are rounded to this. Keep 32 for H3: the latent patch is 2, so a width that is only a multiple of 8 can make the first/last-frame latent odd and the run fails.

inputs.label: Seconds
inputs.help: Up to 40. The frame count is 24 fps rounded up to the H3 5+17n grid (40 s = 974 frames).

inputs.label: Steps
inputs.help: HyperFlow's sigma schedule: 4, 6 or 8 steps at CFG 1.0.

inputs.label: Sparse attention (H3 SLA)
inputs.help: The ROCm SLA node. Off, or on a backend that does not ship it: the node is bypassed and the model goes straight to the sampler.

inputs.label: Sparse attention: detail
inputs.help: 0.85 ignores 85% of blocks (the published run); lower is slower and more exact.

inputs.label: FPS
inputs.help: The model is trained at 24 fps.
